record.original_question: Which components of observed post-burst gamma-ray-burst light curves are genuinely produced by the external forward or reverse shock, and how should jet breaks, chromatic behavior, and reverse-shock signatures be interpreted once internal central-engine contributions are removed? This is especially important in the Swift era, where X-ray afterglows commonly contain multiple components that complicate standard external-shock parameter inference.

evidence.quote: Therefore, in the Swift era, the afterglow modeling made one step backwards: instead of constraining the afterglow model parameters using the data, one needs first to identify which emission component is from the external forward shock, and which is not.
There is no platinum jet breaks identified (i.e. those clearly show achromatic feature in all wavelengths).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider observed multi-wavelength light curves of gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows obtained in the Swift era, where the X-ray and optical emission following the prompt gamma-ray phase is typically modeled as synchrotron emission from a relativistic blast wave decelerating in the circumburst medium (the external forward shock) and, at early times, from a short-lived reverse shock crossing the ejecta, with possible additional contributions from a long-lived central engine (e.g., late prompt emission, plateau, flares).

Define the following:
- An "external forward shock" component is emission whose temporal decay indices α and spectral indices β across bands satisfy the standard closure relations of synchrotron blast-wave theory for a given jet/medium configuration.
- A "reverse shock" component is the short-lived, typically optical/radio early-time emission from the shocked ejecta predicted by Sari–Piran-type models.
- A "jet break" is a steepening of the light curve due to the bulk Lorentz factor dropping below the inverse jet opening angle; it is "achromatic" if the break time and post-break decay slope agree across all observing bands (X-ray, optical, radio), and "chromatic" otherwise. Call a jet break "platinum" if it is verified achromatic across all available bands simultaneously.

The problem: Provide a method, supported by quantitative criteria, to decompose observed Swift-era GRB afterglow light curves into (a) the genuine external forward-shock component, (b) the genuine reverse-shock component, and (c) contributions of internal/central-engine origin, so that:

1. The external-shock parameters (isotropic kinetic energy E, circumburst density n, electron and magnetic energy fractions ε_e and ε_B, electron index p, jet opening angle θ_j) can be reliably inferred only from (a) and (b).
2. One can determine whether any observed light-curve break is a platinum (achromatic across all wavelengths) jet break, and explain the prevalence of chromatic breaks under the proposed decomposition.
3. The reverse-shock signatures (e.g., early optical flash, radio flare) predicted under thin-shell vs. thick-shell regimes can be unambiguously identified or ruled out in each event.

Decide, on the basis of currently available multi-wavelength GRB afterglow data, whether such a decomposition exists in general, and in particular whether any observed jet break to date qualifies as platinum.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent systematic studies (e.g., a 2015 analysis of 85 Swift-era GRBs with well-monitored X-ray and optical light curves) graded events by consistency with external forward-shock predictions and found that simple forward-shock models account for roughly half of GRBs, while up to ~90% can be fit when extended models (long-lasting reverse shock, structured jets, varying medium profiles) are invoked. A small fraction show clearly chromatic behavior incompatible with single-component external-shock models. No truly achromatic ("platinum") jet break across all wavelengths has been unambiguously identified, so the interpretive question remains partially open.

status_evidence.title: How Bad/Good Are the External Forward Shock Afterglow Models of Gamma-Ray Bursts?
status_evidence.snippet: 85 GRBs categorized into five grades; Grade V shows chromatic behaviors inconsistent with external shock models; with advanced modeling >90% may be interpreted within external-shock framework.
status_evidence.claim: Decomposition of Swift-era afterglows into external-shock vs other components is partially achievable but a substantial fraction shows chromatic behavior.

status_evidence.title: Jet Breaks and Energetics of Swift GRB X-ray Afterglows
status_evidence.snippet: Systematic search for jet breaks in Swift X-ray afterglows finds candidate breaks but few unambiguous achromatic cases.

status_evidence.title: Investigating Temporal Features in Swift GRB Afterglows (UVOT/XRT)
status_evidence.snippet: Comparative analysis of UVOT and XRT light curves continues to find chromatic features.
status_evidence.claim: Chromaticity in Swift afterglows is still actively being studied.
